description: A solo-team out here to build, learn, and have fun!
summary:
Lunar VISTA (Visibility & Illumination Site Trade-off Analyzer) is a web app for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates in seconds. Users choose from 65 curated sites (Artemis III candidates, CLPS, other commercial, Apollo and other nations' missions) or enter custom coordinates, and pick a landing time. The app plots the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, built from LRO LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons ephemerides for 2024–2032. For each site it shows time to sunset and Earth-set, 30-day sunlight and Earth-visibility timelines, libration, and 13 metric categories covering power and direct-to-Earth communication. Up to three site-and-date scenarios can be compared side by side, each rated 1–10, with plain explanations of why small changes matter. A toggle adapts the same views for enthusiasts, educators and mission planners.

Why it matters: at the south pole, a few kilometres or a few days can decide whether a lander has sunlight and contact with Earth or neither. Answering that today means working across Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek. Lunar VISTA puts this answer at one place, and every number links to its NASA source, so science & engineering teams can re-plan quickly when a schedule slips.
details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Lunar VISTA is a web app for comparing landing sites and landing dates near the lunar south pole. It has three main pages:

  1. Site selection. You pick a site on a south-pole map, a flat whole-Moon map or a 3D globe. The 65 curated sites cover Artemis candidate regions, CLPS and other commercial missions, Apollo, other nations' landers and named south-pole features. You can also enter custom coordinates. You also choose a landing date and time in UTC.
  2. Site details. This shows the terrain horizon at the site with the Sun and Earth drawn against it. It gives the time to sunset and Earth-set and a 30-day timeline you can scrub or play. There are lanes for sunlight, Earth in view, each Deep Space Network complex, and combined contact time. It also shows libration, a battery and array-power model, and metrics in 13 categories.
  3. Compare. Two or three site-and-date scenarios sit side by side. Each is rated Favourable, Conditional or Unfavourable. A "Why these scenarios differ" row is written from the computed geometry, for example the horizon height toward the Sun at each site.

How it works. Two steps run offline:

  • We pulled hourly Sun and Earth geometry for 2024–2032 from JPL Horizons (DE441) into compact tables. The browser converts these tables into the Sun's and Earth's position in the sky at any site. That conversion matches Horizons' own output to within 0.0002°. Years outside 2024–2032 are fetched live through the server.
  • For each site, we trace 360 rays across the LOLA 120 m polar elevation model out to 200 km. This builds the terrain horizon, including the Moon's curvature and no atmospheric refraction.

The Sun is treated as a disk, so the app shows how much of it clears the ridge, not just whether its centre does. All metric calculations run in the browser, so changing the date or an assumption updates the results straight away.

What are its benefits?

  • One screen instead of several tools. Today you would combine Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek and read their raw output yourself. Here, site, date, horizon, Sun, Earth and DSN coverage are in one place.
  • Fast re-planning. There are ±1-day and ±7-day steps, a side-by-side comparison, and sensitivity metrics: how much sunlit time changes with even a 1-day shift, or a 1 km move.
  • Values you can check. Every number has a tooltip naming its source and status: computed, modelled, reference, assumption or unavailable. Hovering a computed value shows the calculation steps. A metric that can't be backed by data is not shown, rather than estimated.
  • Planners can adjust the model. There are 26 mission assumptions (array, battery, loads, mast height, slope tolerance, link parameters) and 15 sets of rating thresholds. Edits are saved in the browser.
  • Shareable. The site, time and comparison are kept in the URL. There are no accounts, and the history of pages you opened stays in your browser.

What is the intended impact?

For mission planners, the aim is to make "what if we land three days later, or 2 km away?" a question that takes seconds to answer. For educators and the public, the aim is to show why the south pole is so hard: the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, so a ridge a fraction of a degree high can decide whether a site is in light or shadow.

From mission planners to educators to enthusiasts, the level of technicality decreases and the level of explanation increases.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: TypeScript (app and data pipeline), Python (standard-library scripts that build the metric catalog and site list), CSS, Bash.
    • JPL Horizons (DE441), including Goldstone, Canberra and Madrid as observers for DSN visibility
    • LRO LOLA elevation models, plus the LOLA average-illumination maps (used only for validation)
    • LROC permanently shadowed region polygons and the anthropogenic-objects catalogue
    • LRO Diviner polar temperature maps
    • NASA Moon Trek basemap tiles
    • USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature
    • DSN 810-005 handbook (station coordinates, antenna gain)
    • NSSDCA fact sheets
    • 123 quoted values from cited literature
  • Other tools: Git and GitHub, Cursor, Vercel, and Claude Code (AI coding assistant).
  • Hardware: none beyond a laptop.

How is the project creative?

  • One app, three depths. A toggle switches between Enthusiast, Educator and Mission planner. The page structure stays the same and only the level of detail changes. Enthusiasts see 27 metrics framed as plain questions, educators see 89 with explanations, and planners see every available metric plus the assumptions and threshold editors.
  • A horizon you can read. The real skyline, with a partly clipped Sun disk and the Earth on top of it, makes grazing light visible in a way a table of angles doesn't.
  • Communications shown as a timeline. One lane per DSN complex and a combined Contact lane, with handover gaps marked in red.
  • Explanations generated from the data. The comparison explains differences between scenarios using that scenario's own numbers, not fixed text.
  • The app checks itself in public. The Data & methods page shows our results next to an independent NASA product, including where they disagree.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy and authenticity first. No values from memory and no placeholders. 6 candidate sites were left out because I couldn't find a cited coordinate for them.
  • South-pole physics: terrain-limited horizons, the Sun as a disk, no refraction, libration (already included in the Horizons geometry, so it isn't added twice), Earth eclipses of the Sun, and permanently shadowed regions.
  • The schedule-slip scenario from the challenge brief, which shaped the date steps, sensitivity metrics and comparison.
  • Speed and reliability: precomputed tables, because Horizons can't be called directly from a browser, and a 127 MB committed terrain bundle so custom coordinates work without downloading roughly 500 MB of raw data.
  • Readability: light and dark themes, text no smaller than 14 px, and tooltips that open on hover, keyboard focus or tap.
  • Privacy: no accounts or tracking. Preferences and history are stored only in the browser.

How do we know the results are right?

  • The Sun and Earth positions match Horizons' own topocentric output to within 0.0002°.
  • For 35 sites, I compared the share of time the Sun and Earth are above the terrain horizon against LOLA's independent average-illumination maps. The median difference is 0.24 percentage points for the Sun and 0.19 for the Earth. 34 of 35 sites agree within 2 points for the Sun, and 32 of 35 for the Earth.
  • The largest gap is at Malapert Massif: about 9 points for the Sun and 8 for the Earth. LOLA's own map varies from about 15% to 61% within 240 m of that pin, so the result there depends heavily on the exact location.

What are the limitations?

  • The terrain is a 120 m grid, so boulders and metre-scale relief are not modelled.
  • The Artemis region pins are the centres of LROC image mosaics, because NASA does not publish official region centres.
  • The power and link figures are models driven by editable assumptions with example defaults. They don't describe any real lander's hardware.
  • Some rating thresholds follow NASA criteria. Others are planning bands set by this tool, and they are labelled as such.
  • 38 of the 196 metrics are hidden at the reference site because they need mission-specific inputs or measurements taken on the surface.
  • The phone layout isn't finished: the header overflows at about 390 px wide.

Was AI used?

Yes. I built the app with Claude Code, inside Cursor, under my direction. I made the product and design decisions and logged each one in the repo (LOGS.md). Research on site coordinates and reference values was AI-assisted. Every value is stored with its source URL and the quoted text, so it can be checked. No data values are generated by AI.

Who built it?

A one-person team, me, Rounak.

What's next?

  • Finishing the mobile layout.
  • Adding cited sources for metrics that are still unavailable, such as the USGS geologic map and LEND neutron data.
  • Adding the remaining excluded sites once cited coordinates are found.

Where can you try it?

At https://lunar-landing-site-navigator-2026.vercel.app/. It needs no account and no installation. It works best on a desktop browser, because the phone layout hasn't been looked into. The source code is in a public GitHub repo: https://github.com/Not-A-Builder/lunar-landing-site-navigator-2026

Data

You can find all data used in the platform, at https://lunar-landing-site-navigator-2026.vercel.app/sources#sources
Please note: Some data couldn't be attached to the data links for this project due to a cap on the number of links that can be added.

Thank you!
